#10927. ESM vs CommonJS in Node: When to Switch and How to Migrate

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Most Node.js projects still ship CommonJS. That is not a controversial claim; it reflects the inertia of millions of packages built before ES Modules were stabilized in Node 12.22, 14.17 and 15.3. But the ecosystem surrounding those projects — npm packages dropping CJS support, TypeScript defaulting to module settings that emit ESM, bundlers optimizing static import graphs — is accelerating toward ESM-only output. For intermediate Node.js developers maintaining server-side or full-stack production codebases, the question is no longer whether ESM will dominate but when migrating makes sense and how to do it without fracturing a dependency graph or stalling a CI pipeline.

This guide covers the technical differences between CommonJS and ESM in Node.js, the resolution rules that determine how each file is parsed, a checklist for deciding when to migrate, and a staged conversion strategy with concrete error-to-fix troubleshooting references.

Prerequisites: This guide assumes a currently supported Node.js release (Node 22 or Node 24 LTS recommended; Node 18 and 20 have reached end of life). Some features noted below require newer versions, which are called out inline. Examples use bash/zsh shell syntax unless otherwise noted.

Node.js does not guess a file's module format. It checks file extensions, the nearest package.json configuration, and, in narrow cases, a CLI flag.

Files ending in .mjs are always parsed as ES Modules, and files ending in .cjs are always parsed as CommonJS. Files ending in .js are ambiguous on their own; Node.js resolves them by consulting the nearest package.json up the directory tree.

This means that .mjs and .cjs serve as escape hatches. A single CommonJS configuration file can coexist inside an otherwise ESM project simply by using the .cjs extension, and vice versa.

The "type" field in package.json controls how .js files within its scope are parsed. Setting "type": "module" causes all .js files under that package.json to be treated as ESM. Setting "type": "commonjs", or omitting the field entirely, causes them to be treated as CommonJS.

Any .js file within this package's directory tree will be parsed as an ES Module. import and export syntax is expected; require() is not available.

Here, .js files are parsed as CommonJS. require(), module.exports, __dirname, and __filename all work as expected.

The scope boundary is the nearest package.json up the directory tree. In monorepos, this means each workspace with its own package.json controls its own module format independently; the root "type" field does not cascade into workspaces that define their own package.json.

The --input-type flag applies only to non-file input: --eval, --print, and STDIN. It does not affect files on disk.

Note: The --eval snippet above resolves package.json relative to import.meta.url rather than the working directory. This avoids reading an unintended file if the script is invoked from a different CWD. On Windows PowerShell, use a single-line command or a script file instead of multi-line shell syntax.

Without --input-type=module, the import statement in --eval would trigger a syntax error because Node.js defaults to CommonJS parsing for evaluated strings.

CommonJS uses require() for loading and module.exports or exports for exposing values. ESM uses import declarations and export statements. The Node.js modules documentation covers the syntax in detail, but the behavioral implications matter most during migration.

Named exports, default exports, and re-exports (export { foo } from './bar.js') all have direct ESM syntax. CommonJS achieves named exports through object properties on module.exports, which is less amenable to static analysis.

ESM supports top-level await (Node 14.8+ unflagged), allowing modules to perform asynchronous operations at the top scope during evaluation. CommonJS does not support this; asynchronous work at the top level requires callbacks or wrapping in an immediately invoked async function.

The __filename and __dirname globals are not available in ES Modules. The standard replacement uses import.meta.url combined with Node.js built-in utilities (import.meta.url is a file:// URL; fileURLToPath converts it to an OS path string):

import.meta.dirname and import.meta.filename are available natively in Node 21.2+ and Node 20.11+, and the Node docs mark them stable from 22.16 and 24.0. The snippet above uses ?? to fall back to the fileURLToPath pattern on older releases, so it works across all supported versions.

At module scope, this is undefined in ESM, whereas in CommonJS it refers to module.exports.

require() is synchronous. It reads the file, evaluates it, and returns the cached module.exports object. Once loaded, subsequent require() calls return the cached reference. This synchronous nature enables conditional loading patterns like const db = process.env.DB === 'pg' ? require('pg') : require('mysql2').

Node.js statically analyzes and resolves ESM import declarations at link time, before any module code executes; unlike require(), they cannot be deferred to runtime.

Node.js resolves the module graph at link time, not at runtime. ESM named exports provide live bindings: if the exporting module updates a named export's value, importing modules see the change. This does not apply to values captured via default export. CommonJS exports are value copies at the time of require().

The practical implication is that conditional loading in ESM requires dynamic import(), which returns a promise: const { default: pg } = await import('pg').

The "exports" field in package.json lets package authors define entry points with conditions. This lets dual-format packages serve ESM to import consumers and CommonJS to require consumers.

The "types" condition should appear before "default" so that TypeScript resolves type declarations correctly. This ordering is required for TypeScript 4.7+ with moduleResolution: nodenext; earlier versions do not read exports-mapped types at all. If you need to support TypeScript versions before 4.7, add a top-level "types" field in package.json alongside the "exports" map as a fallback. Subpath exports like "./utils" control the public API surface, preventing consumers from importing internal files not explicitly listed.

The "imports" field defines private import aliases scoped to the package itself. Entries must start with # to distinguish them from bare specifiers. For packages that need to support both ESM and CJS consumers (dual-format), use conditional fields:

Inside the package, these aliases work as bare specifiers:

This avoids brittle relative paths like ../../../src/utils.js and centralizes path mappings in one place. If your package is ESM-only (not dual-format), simple string values without conditional fields are sufficient.

If you publish to npm, ship ESM now. Applications can migrate incrementally, module by module. Legacy projects pinned to Node versions below 16 should remain on CommonJS until they can upgrade their runtime floor.

Before changing any configuration, catalog every require() call, entry point, and script in the project. Automated tools such as cjs-to-esm or @babel/plugin-transform-modules-commonjs (in reverse) can flag conversion candidates — verify each tool's maintenance status and test on a branch before applying to production. Manually review test runners, build scripts, and tooling configuration files, many of which (Jest configs, Babel configs, Webpack configs) rely on CommonJS by default.

This step will break any file that still uses require() or module.exports. Have your test suite ready before proceeding.

Add "type": "module" to the root package.json. Then rename any files that must remain CommonJS to .cjs. Common holdouts include tool configuration files that do not yet support ESM.

Only rename config files that actually use CJS syntax. Verify which config files exist first (e.g., ls .eslintrc*), since your project may use a different format (.json, flat config) or may not have these files at all.

Note: Jest does not auto-discover .cjs config files in all versions. After renaming, either pass the config path explicitly (npx jest --config jest.config.cjs) or add "jest": {"config": "jest.config.cjs"} to your package.json to ensure Jest uses the correct configuration.

Replace require() calls with import declarations. Replace module.exports with export statements. Convert dynamic require() to await import().

Note the .js extension on the relative import. ESM requires full specifiers for relative paths; bare specifier resolution only applies to packages listed in node_modules. If the original require('./routes/api') resolved to ./routes/api/index.js, the ESM import must be './routes/api/index.js' — ESM does not perform automatic directory index resolution. The readFile import from the CommonJS version is not carried over because it is not used in this snippet; only import what you use.

If the project is a published library, add a conditional "exports" map as shown in the earlier section. This allows consumers using either require() or import to resolve the correct format.

What does your test runner expect? This step varies by tool, so check each one before making bulk changes.

TypeScript: Set "module" and "moduleResolution" to "nodenext" in tsconfig.json:

Jest: For Jest with ESM, configure transform: {} in jest.config.cjs to disable default Babel transforms. Scope the experimental flag to the Jest invocation rather than setting it globally in NODE_OPTIONS (global settings propagate to all child Node processes, including postinstall scripts):

See Jest ESM docs for the full setup. Alternatively, consider switching to Vitest or Node's built-in test runner (node --test), both of which support ESM natively.

ESLint: The flat config format (eslint.config.js) is ESM-compatible by default (ESLint 8.21+). If using the legacy .eslintrc format, rename it to .eslintrc.cjs.

On Node 22.7+ and 20.19+, syntax detection is on by default: a .js file with no "type" field that contains import or export is treated as ESM. That can hide a missing "type": "module", so set the field explicitly. To confirm that no file relies on detection, run the test suite with --no-experimental-detect-module. Check the flag exists on your version:

Run the full test suite, build pipeline, and any integration tests. A CI smoke test checklist should include: confirming all entry points resolve, verifying dynamic imports load correctly, and ensuring no ERR_REQUIRE_ESM or ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND errors appear in logs.

CommonJS modules can be imported from ESM files using default import syntax. Named imports work only when Node.js can statically detect the CJS module's export keys at parse time — specifically, when the module assigns a static object literal to module.exports. Dynamic assignment (e.g., building the exports object conditionally at runtime) forces default-import-only.

The destructuring happens at runtime rather than through static named imports because lodash's CommonJS exports are assigned dynamically to module.exports. Note that this pattern imports the entire lodash bundle at runtime, which defeats tree-shaking. For ESM-native tree-shaking, use import { groupBy } from 'lodash-es' if your project can take the lodash-es dependency.

Historically, require() could not load ES Modules at all. Current Node releases can: require(esm) is enabled without a flag from Node 22.12 and 20.19, and Node 22.13 and 20.19 stopped printing the experimental warning (see the Node.js modules docs). The call returns the module namespace object, so a default export is under .default. It throws ERR_REQUIRE_ASYNC_MODULE if the ESM graph uses top-level await; use import() in that case.

For older versions, the fallback is dynamic import() inside an async context:

This works on all Node.js versions with ESM support but requires callers to handle the returned promise. The timeout prevents the process from hanging indefinitely if the config module fails to load, and the explicit error handling avoids unhandled promise rejections (which crash the process in Node 15+).

TypeScript mirrors Node.js module resolution through its "module" and "moduleResolution" compiler options. Setting "module": "nodenext" (or "node16") causes TypeScript to emit ESM when the enclosing package.json has "type": "module" and CommonJS otherwise. Setting both explicitly keeps the config clear (newer TypeScript versions infer moduleResolution from module).

The .mts extension produces .mjs output, and .cts produces .cjs output, matching Node.js's extension-based format detection. This allows individual files to opt into a different format than the package default, exactly as .mjs and .cjs do at runtime.

For dual-format library publishing, the build pipeline typically produces two output directories or uses file extensions to differentiate formats. The package.json "exports" map then points each condition to the correct file, with "types" entries referencing .d.ts and .d.cts declarations respectively.

Migrate libraries first, since they impose format constraints on every downstream consumer. Applications can migrate incrementally when their tooling and dependencies are ready. Use the decision table above to justify timing rather than defaulting to either inertia or hype.

CommonJS is not deprecated and remains stable, but the signals point one direction: packages like chalk, got, and execa have dropped CJS entirely, and TypeScript's nodenext resolution treats ESM as the primary target. Waiting is fine. Waiting without a plan is not.

For the canonical reference on Node.js module resolution, package configuration, and interoperability rules, consult the Node.js Packages documentation.

#10920. React Form Validation Using Shared Zod Schemas and Server Actions

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Duplicated validation logic is one of the most persistent sources of bugs in React applications. A client-side rule changes, the server-side copy stays the same, and invalid data slips through the gap. React form validation that relies on a single Zod schema, shared between React Hook Form on the client and a Next.js Server Action on the server, eliminates that drift entirely. This tutorial walks through building that pattern from scratch: a contact form with client-side validation via zodResolver, server-side re-validation with safeParse, accessible error rendering following ARIA authoring practices, and a Vitest test suite that locks down the schema's correctness.

The result is a Next.js App Router contact form where every validation rule lives in one file. When the server rejects a submission, field-level errors map back to individual inputs using setError, and screen readers announce them through aria-describedby associations.

Prerequisites: you should know React, TypeScript, and the Next.js App Router. You will also need Node 20.9 or later, which is the minimum for current Next.js releases. The code below was type-checked with TypeScript 5.9.3 and 7.0.2 and the tests were run with Vitest 5.0.5, React Hook Form 7.90.0, @hookform/resolvers 5.9.1 and Zod 4.6.7.

Start with the standard create-next-app scaffolding. The flags below suppress all interactive prompts and ensure the resulting directory structure matches the file paths used throughout this tutorial:

Each flag matters: --no-src-dir places the app/ directory at the project root (rather than inside src/), and --import-alias '@/*' configures the @/ path alias in tsconfig.json so that imports like @/lib/schemas/contact resolve correctly.

The form layer requires three packages: react-hook-form for state management, @hookform/resolvers for connecting external schema libraries, and zod for schema definition. Testing relies on vitest.

Add @testing-library/react if you plan to write component-level tests beyond the schema tests shown in this tutorial.

After installation, the relevant portion of package.json should look similar to:

The devDependencies block shown is abridged. Your actual file will also contain @types/react, @types/react-dom, @types/node, and ESLint-related packages installed by create-next-app. Those are omitted here for brevity.

The schema lives in its own file so both the client component and the Server Action can import it without pulling in unnecessary dependencies.

Each field carries a custom error message. This tutorial uses Zod 4, where z.email() replaces the deprecated z.string().email(); on Zod 3 keep the older form. The ContactFormData type is inferred directly from the schema with z.infer, so the TypeScript type and the runtime validation rules can never diverge.

Both the client component and the Server Action import contactSchema from this one module. On the client, zodResolver wraps the schema so React Hook Form can evaluate it during its validation cycle. On the server, safeParse() runs the same rules against raw input and returns structured errors without throwing. You author the schema once, but it executes in two runtimes. Any change to a validation rule propagates to both sides immediately.

You author the schema once, but it executes in two runtimes. Any change to a validation rule propagates to both sides immediately.

The complete component is shown below as a single file. It combines the hook setup, the onSubmit handler, and the JSX return in the order they appear in the source.

The useForm hook accepts a resolver option that delegates validation to Zod. Setting mode to 'onTouched' means fields validate on blur and re-validate on subsequent changes, giving users immediate feedback without triggering errors before they interact with a field.

The register function connects inputs to React Hook Form's internal state. errors provides per-field error objects, and isSubmitting tracks whether an async submission is in flight.

Every input receives aria-invalid when its corresponding error exists and aria-describedby pointing to a that holds the error message. The aria-describedby attribute is always present (pointing to a consistently rendered ) so that screen readers maintain the association even when errors are cleared. This follows the ARIA authoring practices for inline error messages: aria-describedby links the error to its input, and aria-invalid signals the error state, so screen readers announce the error when the user focuses the field.

The noValidate attribute on the

element turns off built-in browser validation so Zod's rules run instead. The submit button disables itself during submission to prevent duplicate requests. The aria-busy attribute on the form communicates the loading state to assistive technology.

When React Hook Form's client-side validation passes, onSubmit fires. It calls the Server Action, inspects the response for field errors, and maps any server-returned errors back to individual inputs using the applyServerErrors helper (defined in the "Mapping Server Errors" section below). A try/catch block wraps the handler so that network failures or unexpected Server Action crashes surface as a root-level form error instead of leaving the form stuck in a submitting state.

The type: 'server' string used inside applyServerErrors is a convention, not a React Hook Form requirement. It makes it possible to distinguish server-originated errors from client-originated ones when logging, styling, or routing analytics events.

The Server Action imports the same contactSchema and runs safeParse against the incoming data. If parsing fails, the flattened field errors return to the client. If it succeeds, business logic executes inside a try/catch block to ensure unexpected errors come back as structured responses rather than crashing the action. In a real application, the success branch would perform a concrete operation like inserting a row into a contacts table via Prisma or dispatching a transactional email.

The parameter is typed unknown deliberately. Typing it ContactFormData would let TypeScript accept the data without re-parsing, defeating server-side re-validation.

The z.flattenError() helper turns a ZodError into a flat { formErrors: string[], fieldErrors: { name: string[], email: string[] } } shape, which maps directly to the setError loop on the client. (Zod 3 and 4 also have an error.flatten() method, deprecated in Zod 4.) Zod types each field value as optional via a partial record, so the filtering step above narrows out undefined entries and the returned fieldErrors object is a safe Record.

Client-side validation runs in the browser. A user can bypass it entirely by disabling JavaScript, manipulating form data through DevTools, or submitting requests directly via cURL or an automated bot. Server re-validation using the same schema guarantees that identical rules apply regardless of how the request arrives.

Server re-validation using the same schema guarantees that identical rules apply regardless of how the request arrives.

Implement rate limiting and CSRF token verification alongside schema validation. These complementary measures address different threat vectors, though they fall outside the scope of this tutorial.

The applyServerErrors helper (used in the onSubmit handler above) takes each key from the server's fieldErrors object and injects it into React Hook Form's error state. Because the error spans in the JSX read from formState.errors.fieldName, the correct re-renders automatically and aria-invalid toggles to true on the corresponding input. The accessible error contract stays intact without adding manual DOM queries or event listeners.

For unexpected errors that do not map to a specific field, React Hook Form supports root-level errors via setError('root.serverError', { message: '...' }) (requires react-hook-form >=7.34.0; alternatively use setError('root', ...) on earlier versions). This is useful for handling cases like network failures or internal server errors where no individual field is at fault.

To keep this pattern DRY across multiple forms, the mapping logic lives in a reusable helper. The helper accepts an explicit list of valid field paths and routes any unrecognized keys to a root-level error, preventing server-supplied keys from silently corrupting form state:

This helper is generic over the form's field values type, so it works with any Zod schema and any form that uses React Hook Form. The validFields parameter ensures that only known form field paths are passed to setError, while any unexpected keys from the server response are safely routed to a root-level error. The ContactForm component imports it directly, replacing the inline loop shown in earlier drafts.

Create vitest.config.ts at the project root. This configures the @/ path alias so Vitest can resolve the same imports used in the application code:

Because the schema is a standalone module with no UI dependencies, it can be tested in isolation with fast unit tests. Each test calls safeParse and asserts on the structured result.

These tests assert exact error messages, which catches regressions in user-facing copy as well as validation logic.

Run the full suite with npx vitest run. For continuous feedback during development, npx vitest starts watch mode. Adding either command to a CI pipeline ensures that schema changes are verified on every push.

A single Zod schema, shared between React Hook Form's zodResolver and a Next.js Server Action, eliminates validation drift. The setError mapping closes the feedback loop between server and client. ARIA attributes ensure that error states are perceivable by assistive technology. Vitest locks down the schema's correctness independent of the UI.

A single Zod schema, shared between React Hook Form's zodResolver and a Next.js Server Action, eliminates validation drift.

From here, add file upload validation on the client with z.instanceof(File). Note that server-side file validation requires inspecting FormData entries directly, since uploaded files arrive in the server's FormData rather than in a typed object. You can also integrate useFormStatus from React DOM for streaming submission indicators; this hook must live in a child component of the element, not in the component that renders the form itself. For multi-step forms, split a larger schema across wizard steps using z.pick() or z.omit() so each step validates only its own subset.

For further reading on React Hook Form and Zod, see the relevant guides on SitePoint.

#10914. Modern JavaScript Modules: A Practical Guide to Writing Maintainable Code

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

As web applications grow, JavaScript code can quickly become difficult to manage. What begins as a few functions in a single file may eventually include API requests, user interface logic, validation, data processing, and reusable utilities. Keeping all this functionality in one place makes code harder to understand, test, and maintain.

JavaScript modules provide a structured way to divide an application into smaller, independent files. Each module can expose specific functionality while keeping its internal implementation separate from the rest of the application.

Modern JavaScript supports native modules through import and export, allowing developers to organize code without relying on global variables or manually combining scripts.

This guide explains how JavaScript modules work, how to structure them effectively, and how to avoid common problems when building maintainable web applications.

A JavaScript module is a file that can import functionality from other modules and export its own functions, objects, or values.

Consider a utility function that calculates the total price of a shopping cart. Without a modular structure, this logic might be placed directly inside a large application file.

Instead, create a separate file named cart.js:

The export keyword makes the function available to other modules.

The calculation now exists in one dedicated location. If another part of the application needs the same functionality, it can import the function rather than duplicate the implementation.

This separation also makes the calculation easier to test independently.

JavaScript supports two common export styles: named exports and default exports.

Named exports allow a module to expose multiple explicitly named values.

Another module can import one or both functions:

Named exports are useful for utility files that contain related functions.

A default export represents the module's primary exported value:

It can be imported using a locally chosen name:

Neither export style is universally better. Named exports can make dependencies explicit, while default exports can be convenient when a module has one clear primary purpose.

For a consistent codebase, teams should establish conventions and apply them throughout the project.

Splitting a large file into many smaller files does not automatically improve maintainability. A useful module should have a clear responsibility and a reasonably understandable interface.

For example, an online store might use the following structure:

products.js handles communication with the product API.

cart.js contains shopping-cart operations.

renderProducts.js updates the product interface.

formatCurrency.js formats monetary values.

This structure makes it easier to locate functionality and understand how different parts of the application interact.

The exact organization depends on the project's size. A small website may need only a few modules, while a larger application may benefit from grouping files by feature rather than creating a separate directory for every technical category.

The objective is clarity, not the maximum possible number of files.

A common source of complexity is mixing network requests, data transformation, and DOM updates in a single function.

A more maintainable approach is to place API communication in its own module.

The function checks the HTTP response before attempting to use its data. This matters because fetch() does not automatically reject its promise for HTTP error responses such as 404 or 500.

The interface module can then use the API function:

This example keeps the network request separate from the application entry point.

In a production application, developers would typically add suitable loading states, user-facing error messages, response validation, and any required authentication or caching logic.

It is also important to remember that a separate API module does not replace server-side authorization or input validation.

Static imports are appropriate for dependencies that an application needs as part of its normal execution. However, some functionality is only required after a user performs a particular action.

Dynamic imports allow modules to be loaded when needed.

The report module is requested when the button is clicked rather than being loaded through a static import at the beginning of the application.

This can be useful for analytics dashboards, advanced editors, charts, and other features that are not immediately necessary.

Dynamic imports return promises, so the application should account for loading failures and the delay before the feature becomes available.

For larger applications, bundlers can also use dynamic imports as code-splitting boundaries. This may reduce the amount of JavaScript required for the initial page, although the actual benefit depends on the application's dependency graph and build configuration.

Circular dependencies occur when modules depend on each other, directly or indirectly.

For example, user.js might import a function from permissions.js, while permissions.js also imports something from user.js.

Some circular dependencies can work, but they can make initialization order and module behavior harder to understand. Problems are especially likely when modules access imported bindings before the relevant values have been initialized.

A better design is often to extract shared functionality into a third module.

Instead of importing from each other, the two modules depend on a common utility module.

This approach can reduce coupling and make the dependency structure easier to follow. It is not necessary to eliminate every cycle blindly, but unexpected circular dependencies deserve investigation.

Native JavaScript modules have different loading behavior from traditional classic scripts.

For example, an HTML page can load an application entry point with:

Browsers treat this as a JavaScript module. Module scripts are deferred by default, meaning they are evaluated after HTML parsing rather than blocking parsing in the same way as ordinary synchronous classic scripts.

Modules also have their own scope, so top-level declarations are not automatically added to the global object.

During development, avoid testing module-based pages by simply opening the HTML file through a file:// URL. Browser security restrictions can prevent module imports from working correctly in that environment.

Use a local development server instead. Also verify the correct MIME types and paths when deploying modules to a production server.

One of the main advantages of modular code is that individual functions can be tested without loading the entire application.

For example, the calculateTotal() function can be tested using simple assertions:

This example uses Node.js's built-in assertion module and assumes the project is configured to support ECMAScript modules.

Additional tests should cover edge cases, such as empty arrays, invalid data, and unexpected values, according to the function's intended contract.

API modules can be tested separately from rendering code, while interface modules can be tested for the expected DOM behavior.

Small modules do not automatically guarantee good tests, but clearly defined responsibilities generally make it easier to identify what needs to be tested.

When adopting JavaScript modules, developers should watch for several recurring problems.

Creating modules without clear responsibilities: A file that contains unrelated functions can become difficult to maintain even if it is technically modular.

Duplicating shared logic: If multiple modules implement the same business rule, changes can become inconsistent. Extract genuinely reusable behavior into a shared module.

Using dynamic imports everywhere: Loading every dependency dynamically can introduce unnecessary complexity and delays. Use dynamic imports when deferred loading provides a meaningful benefit.

Ignoring error handling: Network requests and dynamic imports can fail. Applications should handle failures appropriately instead of assuming every operation succeeds.

Overusing shared mutable state: Modules can export objects that multiple parts of an application modify. Uncontrolled shared state can create difficult-to-trace bugs.

Confusing development and production behavior: Module paths, server configuration, and bundler settings should be verified in the actual deployment environment.

JavaScript modules provide a straightforward foundation for organizing modern web applications. Named and default exports make dependencies explicit, separate files clarify responsibilities, and dynamic imports provide opportunities to load optional functionality when required.

The most effective modular architecture is not necessarily the most elaborate. It is one that makes code easy to locate, test, understand, and change without introducing unnecessary dependencies.

By separating API communication from interface logic, keeping module responsibilities focused, and testing individual functions, developers can create JavaScript applications that remain maintainable as their complexity grows.

#10909. Building Accessible Web Interfaces With Modern HTML and CSS

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Accessibility is an essential part of modern web development. A website may look polished and function correctly with a mouse, yet remain difficult to use for people who rely on keyboards, screen readers, magnification, or other assistive technologies.

Building accessible interfaces does not necessarily require complicated frameworks or extensive JavaScript. Many improvements begin with choosing the right HTML elements, providing clear labels, maintaining visible focus indicators, and using CSS that accommodates different user needs.

For developers, the goal is to create interfaces that remain understandable and usable across different devices, input methods, and accessibility requirements.

This article explores practical HTML and CSS techniques that can help make web interfaces more inclusive without adding unnecessary complexity.

Semantic HTML gives elements a meaningful purpose. Browsers and assistive technologies can use this information to communicate the structure of a page to users.

For example, a clickable div might appear to be a button, but it does not automatically provide the keyboard behavior and accessibility semantics of a native button.

It may look like a button after styling, but keyboard support and button semantics must be implemented separately.

A native button is generally a better choice:

Native buttons support keyboard interaction and communicate their role to assistive technologies without requiring custom ARIA attributes.

The same principle applies to navigation links, headings, lists, and form controls. Use elements according to their intended meaning rather than choosing them solely for their default appearance.

Not everyone uses a mouse or touchscreen to navigate a website. Some users rely entirely on a keyboard or an alternative input device that simulates keyboard interactions.

Interactive elements should therefore have a logical focus order and a visible focus indicator.

A simple CSS rule can improve focus visibility:

The :focus-visible pseudo-class allows browsers to display focus indicators when they determine that the indication is appropriate, commonly during keyboard navigation.

Developers should avoid removing outlines without providing an effective alternative. A link or button that receives focus but gives no visual indication can make navigation confusing.

For larger applications, keyboard testing should cover menus, dialogs, dropdowns, forms, and any custom interactive components.

A useful test is to navigate the page using only the Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Space, and arrow keys where appropriate. Users should be able to identify their current position and operate the interface without becoming trapped in an unexpected focus sequence.

Forms are a common source of accessibility problems. Placeholder text alone is not a reliable replacement for a persistent label because it disappears or becomes less visible when users enter information.

An explicitly associated label provides a more dependable structure:

The for attribute on the label matches the input's id, creating an explicit association.

The autocomplete attribute can help browsers recognize the type of information being requested. The required attribute also communicates that the field must be completed.

However, browser validation alone does not guarantee accessible error handling. When validation fails, applications should explain the problem clearly and help users identify the field that needs attention.

For more complex forms, developers can associate additional instructions with controls using aria-describedby and provide appropriate error messages.

Accessible interfaces should accommodate different viewport sizes, text preferences, and reading needs.

Fixed dimensions can cause problems when text becomes larger or content changes length. A card with a fixed height, for example, may clip a heading when users zoom in.

Instead of forcing content into a rigid box, allow the layout to grow:

The clamp() function allows the heading size to scale within a defined range. The line-height gives body text room to breathe, while overflow-wrap helps prevent unusually long strings from overflowing their container.

These settings are starting points rather than universal requirements. Developers should test the actual content, fonts, languages, and supported zoom levels.

Text needs sufficient contrast against its background to remain readable for users with low vision or reduced contrast sensitivity.

A color combination that looks attractive in a design mockup may be difficult to read when displayed on a real device.

For example, consider a secondary label on a white background:

This darker gray generally provides stronger contrast than a very pale gray on white.

Developers should measure actual color combinations rather than relying on visual judgment alone. Under WCAG 2.2, the usual minimum contrast ratio is 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text at Level AA.

Contrast requirements also apply to relevant graphical elements and user interface components. A contrast checker can help identify combinations that need improvement.

Color should not be the only way information is communicated. For example, an invalid field should have a clear error message or another suitable indicator rather than relying solely on a red border.

Animations can improve feedback and communicate changes, but excessive motion may cause discomfort for some users.

CSS media queries allow developers to respect a user's reduced-motion preference:

This example removes the transition and hover movement when reduced motion is requested.

The appropriate response depends on the interface. Some animations communicate important information, so developers should ensure that removing decorative movement does not remove essential feedback or functionality.

Reduced-motion support should be part of the initial design process rather than an afterthought.

Images often communicate information that is not available in surrounding text. Users who cannot see an image need an appropriate text alternative when that information matters.

The alternative text describes the image's relevant purpose rather than listing every visual detail.

Decorative images should generally use an empty alternative:

This allows assistive technologies to skip an image that does not contribute meaningful information.

Complex images, such as detailed charts, may require a longer explanation elsewhere on the page. The alternative text should be based on what users need to understand, not simply on the image filename.

Automated accessibility tools can identify many common problems, including missing labels, some contrast failures, and certain structural issues. However, automated checks cannot determine whether every interaction makes sense to a real user.

A practical testing process should include:

Navigating the interface with a keyboard.

Checking focus order and focus visibility.

Testing forms with missing or invalid information.

Zooming in and checking for clipped content.

Testing meaningful content with a screen reader.

Running an automated accessibility audit and investigating its findings.

The W3C Web Accessibility Initiative provides standards and educational resources for understanding accessibility requirements. WCAG is a useful reference for evaluating web content, but meeting individual technical checks does not automatically guarantee a usable experience.

For important applications, testing with people who use assistive technologies can reveal problems that automated tools and developer assumptions may miss.

Accessible web development begins with thoughtful implementation choices. Semantic HTML, clear form labels, visible keyboard focus, readable typography, sufficient contrast, and reduced-motion support can significantly improve how people interact with a website.

These practices also help create more consistent and maintainable code. Native browser behavior often eliminates the need for custom interaction logic, while clear markup makes interfaces easier to understand and test.

Accessibility should not be treated as a final checklist applied after development. By considering different user needs from the beginning, developers can build web interfaces that are more inclusive, robust, and practical for everyone.

#10903. Modern CSS Grid: Build Responsive Layouts With Less Complexity

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Creating responsive website layouts is a fundamental part of modern front-end development. Developers need interfaces that work across mobile phones, tablets, laptops, and large desktop displays without requiring separate markup for every screen size.

CSS Grid provides a powerful way to organize content into rows and columns. Unlike older layout techniques that often require additional wrappers or complicated positioning, Grid allows developers to define two-dimensional layouts directly in CSS.

When combined with flexible sizing functions, intrinsic layout techniques, and a small number of carefully chosen media queries, CSS Grid can make responsive interfaces easier to build and maintain.

This article explores practical CSS Grid techniques for creating flexible layouts, avoiding common mistakes, and writing cleaner responsive stylesheets.

CSS Grid begins by defining a grid container. Its direct children become grid items, which can be positioned within the resulting layout.

The layout can be defined with a few CSS declarations:

The display: grid declaration establishes the grid formatting context. The grid-template-columns property creates three equal-width columns, while gap controls the spacing between grid items.

This works well when the available space can accommodate three columns. On a narrow screen, however, the columns may become too small. Responsive sizing can solve this without requiring a separate rule for every device.

One useful CSS Grid technique is combining repeat(), auto-fit, and minmax().

This declaration allows the browser to create as many columns as comfortably fit within the available space.

The expression has three important parts:

auto-fit fits available tracks into the grid and collapses empty repeated tracks when appropriate.

minmax() establishes a flexible range for each column.

The nested min(100%, 16rem) also helps prevent the minimum column size from exceeding the container's available width on narrow screens.

As the container grows, more columns can fit. As it shrinks, items naturally move onto additional rows.

This technique is especially useful for product listings, article cards, image galleries, and resource directories.

It does not eliminate the need for testing. Content length, available space, and the desired visual hierarchy may still require additional layout rules.

The auto-fit and auto-fill keywords look similar, but they handle empty repeated grid tracks differently.

With auto-fill, the browser preserves the space for tracks that can fit within the grid, even when there are not enough items to occupy them.

With auto-fit, empty repeated tracks collapse after placement, allowing occupied tracks to expand into the available space.

This can be a good choice for a gallery where a small number of images should expand to fill the available row.

If the design needs to preserve the expected track arrangement even when some positions are empty, auto-fill may be more appropriate.

Neither option is universally better. The choice depends on whether the layout should expand existing items or preserve space for potential additional items.

CSS Grid is also useful for larger page layouts that contain a header, navigation, main content, a sidebar, and a footer.

Grid template areas allow developers to describe this arrangement using named regions.

The corresponding CSS might look like this:

The named areas make the intended layout easier to understand than a collection of unexplained numeric positions.

The minmax(0, 2fr) declaration also helps the main column shrink below its intrinsic content size when necessary, rather than allowing long content to force the entire layout wider.

On smaller screens, the areas can be rearranged:

The same HTML now supports a single-column layout on narrow screens.

One common CSS Grid problem occurs when content forces a column to become wider than expected.

Grid items can have automatic minimum sizes influenced by their content. Long URLs, unbroken strings, wide images, and large code examples may therefore cause overflow.

A practical solution is to allow grid items to shrink:

The zero minimum in minmax(0, ...) gives the tracks more flexibility, while min-width: 0 helps individual grid items shrink when their content would otherwise create an unwanted minimum width.

For code blocks, horizontal scrolling may be preferable to forcing long lines to wrap and changing their formatting.

These techniques address common overflow problems, but the best solution depends on the type of content and how users are expected to interact with it.

Responsive layouts do not always need explicit breakpoints. CSS Grid can often determine a suitable arrangement from the available space and the intrinsic dimensions of its content.

This creates flexible columns with a preferred minimum size of approximately 20rem, unless the container is narrower.

For a card collection, this may be enough to provide a responsive layout without a collection of device-specific media queries.

However, some designs require more deliberate changes. A navigation bar might need to become a menu button, or a sidebar may need to move below the primary content. These are behavioral or structural decisions that intrinsic sizing alone cannot make.

A useful approach is to let Grid handle flexible dimensions and use media queries when the design genuinely needs a different arrangement.

CSS Grid is powerful, but it is not always the simplest tool for the job.

Flexbox is often a better fit for a one-dimensional layout, such as aligning a group of buttons in a row or arranging an icon beside a label.

Grid is generally useful when relationships between rows and columns matter, while Flexbox is particularly effective when content flows primarily along one axis.

Both systems can work together. A page can use Grid for its overall structure and Flexbox for individual components.

The best layout method is the one that expresses the design clearly without introducing unnecessary rules.

A grid that works with three short placeholder headings may behave differently when real content is introduced.

Before shipping a responsive layout, developers should test:

Empty or partially populated card collections.

Intermediate widths where columns begin to feel cramped.

Browser developer tools make it easy to inspect grid tracks and experiment with container dimensions.

It is also useful to test the actual content rather than relying exclusively on idealized examples. Realistic content exposes sizing problems that placeholder text often hides.

CSS Grid provides a flexible foundation for responsive web layouts. Features such as minmax(), auto-fit, named grid areas, and intrinsic sizing allow developers to create adaptable interfaces with relatively little CSS.

The most effective layouts combine these features thoughtfully. Let Grid manage two-dimensional structure, use Flexbox for simpler one-dimensional arrangements, and introduce media queries when the design requires a meaningful change.

By accounting for intrinsic content sizes, preventing overflow, and testing realistic scenarios, developers can build responsive interfaces that are easier to understand and maintain.

#10897. How AI Search Is Changing Property and Local Discovery: What Developers Should Build

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Property searches used to be a list of filters: price, bedrooms, postcode. Increasingly they start as a question typed or spoken in plain language, such as which neighborhoods near good schools have easy transit and a quiet park. AI search tools answer those questions by pulling facts from many pages and combining them. If you build listing sites, local directories, or any location-based product, that changes what "good data" means: your pages are now inputs to someone else's answer.

This article looks at the shift from a developer's point of view. It covers how to model location data so machines can read it, how to generate structured data safely, how to expose neighborhood facts, and how to keep your content crawlable and trustworthy. The code samples are small and meant to be adapted.

A keyword search such as "3 bed house Springfield" maps neatly onto a database filter. A conversational query does not: "somewhere walkable with a library nearby and a short commute" mixes several attributes, some of which your listing form never captured. AI systems work best with pages that state concrete, attributable facts in a consistent structure.

In practice that means three engineering habits:

Structured data in JSON-LD lets search engines and AI systems read a listing without guessing. This function builds the markup from the same record that renders the page, so the two cannot drift apart, and it escapes the output so listing text can never close the script tag early:

Validate the output with the Schema Markup Validator or Google's Rich Results Test during review, and add the check to your test suite so a template change cannot silently break it. Markup must match what visitors can see on the page, otherwise it can be ignored or treated as misleading.

Questions about schools, transport, and local facilities are really questions about distance. If your data lives in PostgreSQL with the PostGIS extension, a radius query on geography types returns distances in meters and is easy to expose as page content or an API field:

Add a spatial index on both geometry columns for production workloads. Then render the results as plain HTML (a short list or table with the source and date) rather than only inside a client-side map widget. A map that needs JavaScript to draw hides the very facts crawlers and AI systems are looking for.

People increasingly ask AI tools to compare properties and to look beyond the asking price, including taxes, utilities, and commute costs. If you publish such figures, publish where they come from. A small convention goes a long way:

This is good engineering hygiene as well as good SEO: it makes stale data easy to find and easy to fix.

Not all discovery starts with a listing. Many people first get a feel for an area from videos and posts by local creators, and AI search surfaces that material too. Vivien Garnès, Co-CEO at Upfluence, puts it this way: "Buyers rarely start with a spreadsheet anymore. Many first learn about a neighborhood from creators filming their commute, their local coffee shop, or a weekend at the park. That kind of content answers the lifestyle questions listings ignore. The smart move is to treat it as inspiration and then check the facts, because a great video can't tell you about school boundaries or property taxes."

The engineering takeaway is to make your own factual pages the place where that inspiration gets verified. If you embed neighborhood videos, give each one a transcript and descriptive surrounding text, and pair it with the structured facts above so the lifestyle story and the checkable details live on the same URL.

Buyers also ask for local professionals and services. For businesses and directories, the basics matter most:

None of the work above helps if crawlers cannot read your pages. Server-render the key facts, make sure important content is not hidden behind interactions that only run in the browser, and decide deliberately which crawlers may access your site. That decision lives in robots.txt:

Check each crawler's documentation for its current user-agent name before adding rules for it, since these change. Also keep an accurate XML sitemap with real modification dates, so updated listings are discovered quickly.

AI search is changing how people ask about places, but the underlying engineering advice is familiar: model your data carefully, say where it came from, and make it readable by machines as well as people. The sites that answer real, specific questions with checkable facts are the ones most likely to be quoted.

#10891. How to prepare for a meta engineer interview

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Two LeetCode mediums in about 40 minutes. That is still the core of a Meta coding round, and most candidates who fail it run out of time rather than not knowing the pattern.

But since October 2025 the loop has picked up a second kind of coding round, one where you get an AI assistant and a multi-file project. A lot of the prep advice online hasn't caught up, so here's how I'd prepare in 2026, round by round.

The process usually runs four to eight weeks from the first recruiter call to a decision. Roughly:

It replaced one of the two traditional onsite coding interviews. You get 60 minutes in CoderPad with a chat panel, and instead of two unrelated puzzles you work through one extended problem with several stages, often starting with getting an existing codebase to run.

You can switch models mid-interview. Candidates have reported GPT-5, Claude Sonnet and Haiku, Gemini 2.5 Pro and Meta's own Llama 4 Maverick.

E3 and E4 candidates often get no design round at all. From E5 up, design carries as much weight as coding, and the behavioral round gets harder because it's partly deciding your level.

Meta's classic coding round is the most predictable interview in big tech, which makes it the most trainable. The question pool leans on a familiar set of topics:

Dynamic programming shows up less than at Google. Don't ignore it, but don't spend a week on it either.

Work through Meta-tagged problems on LeetCode. Premium is worth paying for a month or two, purely for the company tag and frequency sort.

Aim for under 20 minutes per medium, including talking. Many candidates report they couldn't run their code, so practice in a plain editor with no autocomplete, and dry-run your solution on a small input before you say you're done. Interviewers notice when you catch your own bug.

An opinion you can ignore: doing the top 150 Meta-tagged mediums twice beats grinding 300 problems that include hards. Meta rarely asks them, and the second pass is what builds speed.

This is where strong candidates get burned. They assume the round is easier because they have help, then spend 15 minutes reading generated code they don't trust.

What's being measured is still engineering. Can you read unfamiliar code, break the task into pieces, check output, and catch edge cases? Meta has said fairly directly that it's testing classic coding skills, with AI there to make the setting realistic.

The bar is also higher than in a normal coding round. Because you have an assistant, interviewers expect you to get further through the stages than you would alone.

Meta gives you a practice environment before the interview with a sample problem called "the puzzle." Do it. Then practice the shape of the round elsewhere: take a small open-source project, set a 60-minute timer, and add a feature with Cursor or Claude Code while narrating out loud. Hello Interview has a sandbox built around this format too.

Choose your model before the day. Some candidates found GPT-5 too slow under interview pressure and switched to Claude. Whatever you pick, know how it behaves before the clock starts.

Many candidates get to choose between system design and product architecture. Product architecture is about APIs, data models and client-server interaction; system design is about scale, storage and distribution. Backend and infra people should take system design. Product and full-stack engineers usually do better in product architecture.

Alex Xu's System Design Interview (both volumes) is still the standard starting point. After that, Hello Interview's write-ups of common questions like news feed, chat, Instagram and top-K.

Meta likes questions that look like its own products, so practicing "design the Facebook News Feed" is homework, not cheating.

Candidates who burn 20 minutes on requirements never reach that last step, and it's the part that separates E5 from E6.

It's easy to treat this round as a chat. It isn't. Meta scores it on specific signals, including handling conflict, driving work through ambiguity, learning from failure and the size of your impact, and at senior levels it feeds directly into leveling.

Write six to eight stories from the last three years. Each one should contain a number: latency cut from 800ms to 200ms, a launch that reached 2 million users, five engineers across two teams you got aligned. Map every story to two or three signals so you can reuse them.

Use STAR loosely. Interviewers interrupt with follow-ups, so know the details cold: who disagreed with you, what you'd do differently, what actually happened afterwards.

It's the most common mistake in this round. They want to know what you did.

Solo practice gets you to knowing the material. Mock interviews get you to performing it while someone watches, and that gap is where most people fail. You probably want a mix of AI, human and peer mocks.

These are the cheapest way to get volume:

The upside is that you can do one at 11pm on a Tuesday, and they're good at drilling the habit most people neglect, which is thinking out loud. The downside is that quality varies a lot and AI interviewers tend to be generous with hints and praise. Take their scores with a grain of salt. Also helps if you follow an interview guide for a Meta Engineer

A general assistant works surprisingly well. Give Claude or ChatGPT (voice mode is good for this) a prompt like:

You're a Meta E5 interviewer. Ask me one medium problem from Meta's usual topics, give no hints unless I ask, interrupt with follow-ups, and at the end grade me harshly on communication, correctness and time.

It's especially useful for behavioral practice if you tell it to dig into your stories the way a skeptical engineering manager would.

interviewing.io runs anonymous mocks with engineers from Meta and other large companies, and it's the closest you'll get to the real loop. Paid coaching usually costs $100 to $200 an hour.

Peer mocks through Discord groups, Reddit or a friend at another company are free and much better than nothing.

AI mocks for the first few weeks to build the narrating habit, then two or three human mocks in the last two weeks, at least one of them for design.

If you're working full time, give yourself six to eight weeks.

Ask your recruiter for more time if you need it. Meta recruiters push dates by a few weeks all the time, while a rejection usually means waiting six months to a year before you can reapply (one recent candidate was told a full year). Taking the interview before you're ready is the most expensive mistake in the whole process.

#10884. Top Accessibility Errors in Production and How to Avoid Them

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Most accessibility problems on a website aren't hard to fix. Low-contrast text. An image with no alt text. A button that doesn't tell a screen reader what it does. None of these need a rebuild or a specialist.

Every year, WebAIM scans the home pages of the top million websites and checks them against basic accessibility standards. The 2026 report found that almost 96% of the pages scanned had at least one automatically detectable accessibility failure.

What stands out even more is what the errors actually are. The same problems have topped this report for seven years in a row. These aren't new, complex edge cases; they are the same simple, repeating mistakes.

In this guide, we'll look at what those top errors actually are, why they keep making it to production, and the simple workflow habits you can use to catch them before your users do. We'll also cover where tools like TestMu AI's Accessibility Testing Suite fit into that workflow.

It's easy to assume teams just don't care. But that's rarely the reason. Most developers know what alt text is for. Most designers know low contrast is a problem. The real issue is simpler; a few patterns explain most of it:

None of these come from not knowing accessibility rules. They come from how software is actually built: fast, in multiple moving pieces, with much of the page assembled from components and third-party code that nobody on the team wrote from scratch.

WebAIM's report found that a small number of accessibility issues account for most detectable WCAG failures across the top one million websites. The sections below explain what each issue is, why it matters, and how to fix it.

This is the single most common accessibility error, appearing on nearly 84% of homepages, according to WebAIM.

Poor contrast means the text color is too close to the background color, making it hard to read. For instance, light gray text (#999) on a white background (#FFF) yields a contrast ratio of 2.85:1, which is well below the standard requirement. For anyone with low vision or color blindness, that text becomes unreadable.

The Fix: WCAG asks for a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for normal text. Running a quick check with tools like the WebAIM Contrast Checker or a Lighthouse audit will give you the exact ratio before your page ships. Because the tools lay it out so clearly, this is easily one of the quickest errors on this list to catch and fix.

This is the second most common accessibility error, appearing on more than half of the homepages scanned by WebAIM.

Alt text is the written description a screen reader reads out loud in place of an image. Without it, a screen reader either skips the image entirely or announces the file name, which tells a user nothing about the image.

For example, if it's a product photo, a chart, or an icon that functions as a button, missing alt text means a screen reader user has no idea what they're looking at, what it does, or what happens when they click it.

The Fix: Describe what the image actually shows instead of just saying it's an image. If it's purely decorative and adds nothing a screen reader user needs, use an empty alt attribute (alt="") instead of leaving it off. That tells the screen reader to skip it cleanly.

Missing form labels appeared on 51% of home pages. This one is easy to miss because the form inputs often still look labeled. A form field looks perfectly labeled on screen when the label is simply placed next to the input box. A sighted user sees "Email" written next to a box and knows what to enter.

A screen reader, however, doesn't rely on visual placement. It relies on the HTML. If "Email" isn't actually connected to that input field in the markup, the field may be announced as simply "edit text" or "blank," leaving the screen reader user with no indication of what information it expects.

Placeholder text isn't a substitute either because it disappears as soon as the user starts typing.

The Fix: Associate every form control with a visible

Nearly half of all homepages contain links with no accessible name. The most common examples are icon-only links, such as a search icon, shopping cart, or social media icon. Sighted users recognize these icons immediately, but a screen reader may announce them simply as "link," giving users no indication of what each one does.

The Fix: Give every icon-only link an accessible name using visible text, aria-label, or another appropriate labeling method. This preserves the visual design while allowing screen readers to announce the link's purpose.

About 31% of home pages have buttons with no accessible name, and the share has risen every year since 2021. The usual culprits are icon-only buttons: a hamburger menu, a close "X" on a modal, a play button, or a carousel arrow. A screen reader announces these as just buttons, so users can't tell whether they open a menu, close a dialog, or submit a form.

The Fix: Give every button an accessible name. Use visible text where you can. For icon-only buttons, add aria-label (for example, aria-label="Close dialog") or visually hidden text inside the button. If the icon is an image, provide alt text that describes the action, not the image.

Around 14% of homepages don't specify the page's language. Without it, screen readers have to guess how the text should be pronounced, which can result in words being read with the wrong pronunciation or accent.

The Fix: Set the page's language using the lang attribute on the root element. For example, . It's a one-line change that helps screen readers interpret the entire page correctly.

Many users rely on a keyboard instead of a mouse to navigate a website. If a menu only opens on hover, a custom dropdown only responds to clicks, or a button can't receive keyboard focus, those controls become unusable for them.

The Fix: Every interactive element should be reachable with Tab and Shift+Tab and operable with the keys users expect: Enter for links and buttons, Space for buttons and checkboxes, arrow keys inside menus, tabs, and radio groups, and Escape to close dialogs and menus. You can test this by trying to navigate the entire page using only the keyboard.

Developers sometimes remove the browser's default focus outline to improve the visual design but don't replace it with another focus style. As a result, keyboard users can no longer tell which element is currently selected as they move through the page.

The Fix: Never remove a focus outline without providing a clear replacement. Every interactive element should have a visible, high-contrast focus indicator that tells keyboard users where they currently are on the page.

Videos without captions exclude people who are deaf or hard of hearing and make content harder to follow when audio isn't available or practical. Captions also help users understand speech in noisy environments or when the audio quality is poor.

The Fix: Provide accurate captions for every video. If the video contains important spoken information, include a transcript as well. Automatically generated captions are a good starting point, but they should always be reviewed for accuracy.

On mobile, small buttons and links are hard to hit accurately. Users may tap the wrong control, trigger an unintended action, or have to try multiple times before the touch registers. WCAG 2.2 Level AA sets a minimum target size of 24x24 CSS pixels, with 44x44 CSS pixels recommended (WCAG AAA and Apple's own guidance).

The Fix: Give every tappable element enough size and padding to be reliably tappable, even if the visible icon inside it remains small. Aim for 44x44 CSS pixels, and never go below 24x24.

Run a scanner across a page, and it catches a good chunk of what's wrong. Missing alt attributes, contrast ratios below the required threshold, a form field with no label in the code. Automated scanners catch these immediately.

According to most industry estimates, automated tools catch about 30 to 40 percent of accessibility issues. That's worth running. It also means most of what actually breaks a page isn't something a scanner can see at all.

Take alt text, for instance. A scanner can confirm an image has an alt attribute. It can't tell you if that attribute says anything useful. "Image description here" and an actual description of the photo both pass the same check because the tool only confirms the field isn't empty.

Take another example of a custom div button with role="button". A scanner sees the role and perceives it as a button. It has no way of knowing that nobody added the keyboard handling that makes the button actually work, because that's not something a static scan can test. You'd only catch it by unplugging your mouse and tabbing through the page yourself.

Reading order works the same way. A page can pass every automated check and still present its content in an order that makes no sense once you strip away the layout and just listen to it, top to bottom.

None of this means automated tools aren't worth using. It means they're a baseline, not a final check. Treating a clean scan as proof that a page works is exactly how these errors keep making it to production in the first place.

Most of the errors covered here aren't difficult to fix on their own. The harder part is catching them before they enter your codebase. The best time to find these problems is while you're designing, building, and reviewing a feature, not right before a release.

Automated testing should be part of that process. It catches common issues quickly, right as they're introduced, but it isn't a substitute for manual testing. A clean scan only tells you that no automatically detectable issues were found.

That's where platforms like TestMu AI (formerly LambdaTest) come in. TestMu AI's Accessibility Testing Suite is built around that split. Its axe-core-powered scanner can run on every build in your CI/CD pipeline, on a schedule to catch issues introduced by content or third-party updates, and inside your IDE through its MCP server. For the checks automation can't cover, you can test manually with real screen readers, including NVDA, VoiceOver, and TalkBack, and with keyboard navigation, so a person can confirm what users actually hear and can reach.

If your team writes code with AI coding agents, you can bring those checks into the same workflow with TestMu AI's accessibility agent skill. It's an instruction pack from TestMu AI's open-source agent-skills repository that teaches agents like Claude Code, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, or Gemini CLI how to add WCAG scanning to an existing Selenium, Playwright, or Cypress suite. You tell the agent which pages to scan, and it wires the checks into your framework and runs them on the TestMu AI cloud, with each scan's issues and WCAG mappings in your Accessibility dashboard. A passing scan still isn't the whole job, which is why the manual checks below matter.

Before shipping, spend a few minutes using the page yourself. Navigate using only the keyboard and verify that the focus indicator remains visible. If your site includes forms, menus, or dialogs, ensure they work without a mouse. For critical user journeys, testing with a screen reader will surface issues no automated tool can flag.

Finally, if the same issue keeps recurring, update your design system, component library, or review process to prevent it from happening again. Preventing a bug at the root is always easier than fixing it repeatedly.

Every error in this piece affects a real person trying to use your site. Low contrast text means someone with low vision can't read what you've written. A missing form label means someone using a screen reader can't fill out the form at all. These aren't rare situations; they happen constantly, on ordinary pages, to people who are simply trying to use your product.

That's what accessibility actually comes down to. It is not just a standard to meet, but the same usability you already care about, extended to people who navigate a page using assistive technologies.
